*STATEMENT: Escalating Digital Censorship in India*

*New Delhi, February 28, 2026*

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) is concerned by a cluster of online blocking and takedown actions and ISP level service disruptions reported between 24–28 February 2026. Across these incidents, users and affected services face restrictions without clear, timely reasons and without access to the underlying orders needed to challenge state action by exercising their rights to obtain legal remedy.

Developers reported severe, uneven disruption in access to Supabase across multiple Indian networks. Reporting indicates the disruption followed a government direction, with accounts suggesting use of Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Yet there has been no public statement of the grounds, scope, or duration, and no accessible order for those impacted. Supabase has publicly stated that its domains became inaccessible due to a “ministry order”, and users have been pushed to workarounds such as alternative DNS or VPNs. In parallel, users on X (formerly Twitter) continue to receive “withheld in India” notices restricting specific posts within the country. Such notices usually do not provide the government order or its reasoning. Hence, for those who are being censored the basics of natural justice of a notice, opportunity for a hearing and remedy are delayed or absent.

This is enabled by secrecy built into the blocking framework. Section 69A is implemented through the 2009 Blocking Rules, which contemplate a committee process and, where feasible, notice to intermediaries and identifiable originators. But they also impose “strict confidentiality” over requests and actions taken. When orders and reasons are secret by default, affected persons cannot test legality, necessity, proportionality, or factual errors except through protracted litigation. When in _Shreya Singhal v. Union of India_ (2015), the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A while relying on the existence of procedural safeguards and reasoned decisions, indicating that impacted users could approach court in writ remedies. However, due to the operational secrecy and providing copies of orders and notices those who are censored and prevented from obtaining judicial remedy.

The February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules, 2021 further increase these risks. The substituted Rule 3(1)(d) requires intermediaries to remove or disable access within three hours of receiving “actual knowledge”, which can arise from a court order or a written “reasoned intimation” by authorised government officers. While the rule lists what a “reasoned intimation” should contain, the legal basis, statutory provision, nature of the unlawful act, and specific URL/identifier, the three-hour window pressures platforms to comply promptly which may often occur without any substantive assessment. These inherently opaque censorship practices are being accelerated through "Sahyog" portal. Developed by the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), the Sahyog portal operates entirely without statutory footing, only being anchored in the IT Rules, 2021 that are created by executive notification. It functions as a censorship clearinghouse that deliberately bypasses the established, albeit weak, procedural safeguards of Section 69A. By routing automated takedown directives directly to intermediaries under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, the portal structurally excludes citizens and impacted users from the grievance process.

We demand that the government introduce strictly judicially enforceable transparency requirements, publish all blocking orders, and restore the principles of natural justice to India's platform governance framework. Based on requests from our community we will also next week launch a rough public sheet in which social media users can input and add information on digital censorship.

One Blocking Order Every 68 Seconds: When the State Starts Controlling the Digital Public Square

[The News Minute — 1.95 lakh blocking orders in five months]
https://t.co/4pKxvmx3EL

The number is staggering:

Nearly 1.95 lakh government blocking directions to Instagram, Facebook and YouTube between March and July 2026 — roughly one every 68 seconds. 

And there is an important caveat: 1.95 lakh blocking orders do not necessarily mean 1.95 lakh individual posts were removed. A single order can cover hundreds of posts, accounts or pieces of content. 

But even with that qualification, the scale demands serious democratic scrutiny.

The distribution is striking:

Instagram: nearly 1 lakh orders

Facebook: around 80,000

YouTube: nearly 15,000

Most were routed through the Union Home Ministry's Sahyog portal. Meta has also integrated its systems with the portal, allowing flagged material to be removed automatically in response to government directions. 

And the timing cannot simply be ignored.

These five months overlapped with the student protests over examination irregularities, during which social media became an important tool for mobilisation and public discussion. Reporting has also documented takedowns involving posts supporting the protests and criticism of government policies. 

There is another crucial legal distinction that must not be lost in the political debate:

These 1.95 lakh directions should not all be described as Section 69A blocking orders. A significant proportion were issued through Sahyog under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, which operates differently from Section 69A. 

That distinction makes the central democratic question even more important:

Who decides what citizens are allowed to see, question and share — and what independent mechanism exists to challenge that decision?

A democratic government unquestionably needs mechanisms to tackle deepfakes, fraud, cybercrime, incitement and genuinely unlawful content.

But those powers must come with transparency, due process, accountability and meaningful avenues of appeal.

Because social media is no longer merely entertainment.

It is where citizens organise, protest, educate one another, expose wrongdoing, criticise governments and participate in democracy.

When the machinery capable of silencing digital speech operates at the rate of one government blocking direction every 68 seconds, every citizen should be asking:

What is being blocked?
Why is it being blocked?
Who ordered it?
And who watches the people doing the blocking?

A democracy should never fear citizens who question power.

It should fear a system in which citizens become afraid to question it.

The Cockroach Janta Party, founded by Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) member Abhijeet Dipke, has compromised the sensitive personal information of people who were misled into believing that he was fighting for the cause of ‘students’ in the aftermath of the NEET paper leak.

For the unversed, Dipke had called upon his followers to register on his party’s website :
https://t.co/KlVSTjKcp6
soon after it was launched.

Later, the AAP member alleged that the government took down his website, a claim that was later found to be false. It has now come to light that the users who trusted Abhijeet Dipke with their personal information have now been left vulnerable at the hands of potential cybercriminals.

On Wednesday (1st July), OSINT expert Nisarga took to X (formerly Twitter) to expose vulnerabilities on the website of the Cockroach Janta Party.

Earlier in its brief existence, the site was live and then responded with standard HTTP 403 errors from Hostinger’s active servers before the hold took effect.

In domain management terms, “clientHold” is a standard EPP (Extensible Provisioning Protocol) status code controlled exclusively by the registrar, not by governments or external authorities. According to ICANN documentation and registrar policies, this status instructs the registry not to publish the domain in the DNS, effectively taking it offline until the registrar resolves the underlying issue. Such instruction can be issued only by the owner of the website, not third parties, not even governments. Alternately, the domain provider or the host can take the website offline due to various reasons.

It is commonly applied for routine administrative reasons such as incomplete WHOIS contact verification, billing or payment problems, compliance violations, or at the request of the domain owner. The clientHold affects resolution globally at the registry level, not at any country level.

On the other hand, when a government orders blocking a website, it is done through ISPs (Internet Service Providers) in the country, and the block only takes place in that country. In India, such a block is typically enforced through the Department of Telecommunications via ISP-level DNS poisoning, IP blacklisting, or URL filtering. Such actions allow the domain to still resolve correctly on international resolvers outside the country. That is why websites blocked by the Indian govt can be accessed in India through VPN.

Moreover, when one visits a website blocked by the govt, the browser displays a message saying the same. But when one visits cockroachjantaparty’s website, the browser displays the code DNS_PROBE_FINISHED_NXDOMAIN. This means the browser can’t find the domain because it has been deactivated.

Moreover, no public government orders, court directives, or official statements have been issued regarding https://t.co/n5u5L8JbZ5, further undermining the censorship claim.

Therefore, the analysis of the website shows that either it has been taken by Dipte himself, or the domain provider/host took it down due to some compliance issues. There is no evidence that the site was taken down on Indian government’s order.

Statement : IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. No suspension order has been made public.

New Delhi, 20 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services imposed today, 20 July 2026, in parts of Central Delhi, including the area around Jantar Mantar. The shutdown coincided with the 'Chalo Sansad' march called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) on the opening day of the Monsoon Session of Parliament, where thousands of students and young people had gathered to press their demands. Permission for the march was refused. Prohibitory orders were imposed under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. Routes to Parliament were sealed, and metro stations including, Patel Chowk, Rajiv Chowk and Janpath were closed. Amid reports of the use of force to disperse protesters, mobile internet was then switched off, reportedly "as a precautionary measure". We urge the immediate restoration of all telecommunication services in the capital and an end to internet shutdowns across India.

The developments of today are of immense consequence to the future of our democracy. The voices gathered at Jantar Mantar, and the residents of the national capital, need to be heard the loudest, not silenced en masse.

No order has been made public

At the time of release of this statement, no copy of any suspension order has been published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. Residents of the capital do not know which authority directed the shutdown, on what grounds, over which precise areas, for which services, or for what duration. An unpublished order is an unaccountable order. It cannot be challenged before a court, and the judicial review guaranteed by the Supreme Court becomes illusory. Some reports further indicate the deployment of network jammers in parts of Central Delhi, including near Jantar Mantar. Jamming equipment finds no sanction in the legal framework for the suspension of telecommunication services at all. If jammers were deployed, the government must disclose under what legal authority.

Binding safeguards violated

On 10 January 2020, the Supreme Court in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637 held that the freedom of speech and expression, and the freedom to carry on trade or business through the medium of the internet, are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. The Court directed that every order suspending telecom services must be published. Reasons must be recorded in writing. The restriction must be proportionate, adopting the least restrictive measure available. It cannot continue indefinitely. It is subject to judicial review, and to scrutiny by a review committee.

Parliament has since replaced the framework of the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023, telecommunication services may be suspended only on the occurrence of a public emergency or in the interest of public safety, on the grounds specified in that provision, and for reasons recorded in writing. The Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, notified on 22 November 2024, give effect to this power. A suspension order may be issued only by the Union Home Secretary or the State Home Secretary. An officer not below the rank of Joint Secretary may act in unavoidable circumstances, subject to confirmation by the competent authority within twenty four hours. Every order must clearly define the geographical area and the specific services suspended, and cannot remain in operation beyond fifteen days. Every order must also be published. A Review Committee must meet within five days of the order and record its findings on whether it complies with Section 20(2).

These safeguards are not being followed

If we account for today's shutdown against this legal architecture. The order is unpublished, in breach of Anuradha Bhasin and the Suspension Rules, 2024 alike. No recorded reasons are available to the public despite little to no reports of violence and consistent calls for the protest to be peaceful by the CJP and other organisers. The precise areas and services covered are undisclosed and so is the duration. Whether the competent authority even issued the order cannot be known. Whether the Review Committee will examine it cannot be verified. While the Suspension Rules prescribe no outer time limit for publication, a gap we have previously flagged, it cannot cut against the spirit of the Anuradha Bhasin judgement. A blanket suspension across densely populated parts of the capital, imposed as a "precaution" against a march to Parliament, is the opposite of a narrowly tailored, least restrictive measure. A shutdown timed to a protest restricts the freedoms of speech and assembly at the very moment they matter most.

The human cost of a shutdown

Access to the internet is a digital right on which the exercise of our fundamental freedoms now depends. When the network goes dark in Central Delhi, a journalist at Jantar Mantar cannot file her report or broadcast live. A street vendor on the surrounding roads cannot accept a UPI payment. A gig worker loses a day's earnings. A parent cannot confirm that a child who joined the march is safe. Cutting off communications prevents people from reaching out for help and manufactures panic in a moment which demands calm. These costs fall hardest on daily wage earners and small traders who can least absorb them. Internet based communications also promote trust between people and their government. 

A pattern, not an aberration

Delhi has seen this before. On 19 December 2019, mobile services were suspended for the first time in the capital's history during the protests against the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, in areas including Seelampur, Jamia Nagar and Mandi House. On 26 January 2021, the Ministry of Home Affairs suspended internet services in Singhu, Ghazipur, Tikri, Mukarba Chowk, Nangloi and their adjoining areas during the farmers' protests. According to the #KeepItOn coalition's report released in March 2026, India recorded 65 internet shutdowns in 2025, the highest of any democracy in the world, and accounts for 920 of the 2,102 shutdowns documented globally since 2016. We have consistently advocated against the harm these disruptions cause, from Jammu and Kashmir to Rajasthan, and from Haryana to Manipur, where a shutdown in 2023 ran for over two hundred days. The orders are rarely published on time, and the findings of review committees never see daylight.

Our demands

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore all suspended telecommunication and internet services in Central Delhi.
2. Publish forthwith every suspension order passed on or around 20 July 2026, together with the reasons recorded in writing, as mandated by Anuradha Bhasin and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024.
3. Disclose the issuing authority, the grounds, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation, and clarify whether network jammers were deployed and under what legal authority.
4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days as required by the Rules, and make its findings public.
5. Reform Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 to provide for independent prior authorisation and real consequences for unlawful suspensions.

IFF will file applications under the Right to Information Act, 2005 seeking copies of the suspension orders and the records of the Review Committee, and is examining further legal remedies. 

Delhi and all of India deserve better.

You seem to have learned RSS history either from WhatsApp forwards or inherited RSS talking points—and forgotten to examine the historical record. So before presenting the RSS as the guardian of Indian patriotism, let us review the documented facts.

1/ The RSS was founded in Nagpur in 1925 by K.B. Hedgewar. Although Hedgewar had participated personally in anti-colonial politics, the RSS did not institutionally join major Congress-led movements such as Quit India in 1942. Some individual members participated independently.

2/ In 1939, We, or Our Nationhood Defined was published under future RSS chief M.S. Golwalkar’s name. It praised Nazi Germany’s “race pride” and described its persecution of Jews as “a good lesson for us in Hindusthan.” The RSS later rejected the book as authoritative.

3/ On 14 August 1947, the RSS-linked Organiser criticized the Tricolour and predicted that it would “never be respected and owned by Hindus.”

4/ The Government of India banned the RSS on 4 February 1948 following Gandhi’s assassination, alleging that members had participated in violent and unlawful activities. No court found that the RSS organization had planned Gandhi’s murder.

5/ In a September 1948 letter to RSS leader Golwalkar, Home Minister Sardar Patel accused the organization of spreading “communal poison.” He also alleged that RSS members celebrated Gandhi’s assassination and distributed sweets.

6/ The ban was lifted in July 1949. By then, the RSS had adopted a written constitution. The government announced that Golwalkar had clarified the organization’s commitment to peaceful methods and loyalty to India’s Constitution and national flag.

7/ On 30 November 1949, after the Constituent Assembly adopted India’s Constitution, an Organiser editorial complained that the document contained “nothing Bharatiya” and criticized its failure to draw upon the laws of Manu.

8/ The RSS was banned again during the Emergency in 1975, when it participated in resistance to Indira Gandhi’s authoritarian rule. It was banned a third time following the Babri Masjid demolition in 1992; that ban was later lifted by a tribunal.

9/ The Bharatiya Jana Sangh—the BJP’s predecessor—was established in 1951 with extensive participation from RSS members. Multiple BJP leaders, including Narendra Modi, began their political careers as RSS pracharaks.

These are matters of documented history—not opinions about Hinduism or allegations against individual Hindus.

These have become some of the most ordinary sentences in Indian life. That ordinariness is the achievement. Successful infrastructure is not technology displayed as spectacle; it is technology absorbed into everyday life and trusted without a second thought.

Exactly ten years ago, UPI was rolled out. India did not merely introduce another way to pay, it began transforming the relationship between citizens, commerce and money.

As a Chartered Accountant, I tend to trust numbers more than adjectives. In FY 2016–17, UPI processed approximately 1.8 crore transactions worth about ₹0.07 lakh crore. By FY 2025–26, that had risen to 24,161 crore transactions worth ₹314 lakh crore.

In July 2026 alone, UPI processed 2,365 crore transactions worth ₹29.88 lakh crore: an average of approximately 76.3 crore transactions every day.

These figures tell us how far UPI has travelled.

UPI’s real achievement is that it made sophisticated financial infrastructure almost invisible. The same interoperable payments rail now serves a street vendor and a large retailer. A small entrepreneur receives money instantly. A family can transfer funds across the country in seconds. A student in a hostel can receive ₹500 from home before the phone call ends.

By June 2026, UPI had onboarded 55.49 crore users. The Government has also reported that it serves 6.5 crore merchants, while 741 banks were live on the platform by July. During FY 2025–26, UPI accounted for nearly 86% of India’s retail payment transactions by volume. An IMF Fintech Note describes it as the world’s largest retail fast payment system by volume.

text:
The Indian middle class is the most risk-averse sections of society. There are good historical reasons for this. A large part of the generation that is now above 30 or 35 grew up in scarcity, with limited money, limited opportunities and very little social security. India had a huge population competing for relatively few jobs, houses, educational opportunities and other basic resources. For many families, one serious financial setback could undo decades of progress.

That environment created two very different responses. One group learned to exploit the system. The corrupt politician, contractor, middleman, bureaucrat and businessman figured out that in a system where resources were scarce and institutions were weak, power could be converted into money and money could be converted back into more power. They became comfortable operating in the grey areas of the system.

The other group learned almost the opposite lesson. They became extremely protective of whatever they managed to build. Get a stable job, buy a house, educate the children, save money, pay taxes, follow the rules and, most importantly, stay away from trouble. Don't get into an unnecessary fight with the police. Don't antagonise the local politician. Don't get into a dispute with a contractor. Don't challenge the municipality unless absolutely necessary. Keep your head down and protect what you have.

This psychology did not disappear even with financial success. A person may own a house worth several crores, pay lakhs in school fees, earn a good salary, run a successful business and have substantial savings, but still carry the same underlying fear. There is always a feeling that one wrong move, one confrontation with the wrong person or one unexpected legal or administrative problem could put years of hard work at risk.

This fear has kept a large part of the middle class away from active public life and politics. They may have strong opinions about corruption, bad roads, illegal construction, poor municipal services or political incompetence, but usually prefer discussing these things among friends rather than getting involved directly. It is not necessarily because they don't care. In many cases, they simply feel that the cost of getting involved is too high.

This creates a very comfortable environment for the more aggressive parts of the system. Contractors can build poor roads because they know public resistance will be limited. Builders can violate norms because enforcement is often negotiable. Local politicians can operate with considerable freedom because the people most capable of challenging them are also the people most concerned about protecting their own lives and assets.

The running record of Trump 2.0 that America cannot afford to forget.

Trump says U.S. partnerships gained majority control over vast reserves; Venezuela says it retains ownership. The deal is documented, but illegality or corruption is not established.

• August 29, 2026 — Trump imposed 50% tariffs on about $20 billion in Canadian imports under an apparently untested Depression-era law after his earlier tariff authority was rejected. Canada retaliated; the new legal theory has not been adjudicated.

• August 29, 2026 — DHS used a customs statute to obtain six months of journalist Georgia Fort’s phone records and seek records involving journalists, nonprofits and unions without prior judicial approval. The demands are documented; their legality remains unresolved.

• August 28, 2026 — A federal judge ruled that using immigration law to revoke visas or pursue deportation over pro-Palestinian advocacy or criticism of Israel violated the First and Fifth Amendments.

• August 26, 2026 — A federal judge rejected DOJ’s request to erase Steve Bannon’s contempt-of-Congress conviction for defying the Jan. 6 committee, finding prosecutors had not shown dismissal served justice. DOJ may try again; Bannon already served four months.

• July 2026 — The administration sharply increased wild-horse removals and sales; reporting indicates some federally protected horses may have entered the slaughter pipeline. BLM says it does not knowingly sell horses for slaughter.

1. THAT recently, a digital broadcast / video recording was published and circulated on social media platform Instagram at (URL-https://t.co/23wqH3iWHY),featuring you, the unidentified Noticee (Jane Doe).

1.1 THAT in the aforementioned video broadcast, you have publicly uttered, performed, and disseminated statements/actions that are defamatory, inciting public mischief, & outraging public sentiments , hereby causing grave injury to public peace .

2. Your acts and public utterances attract strict criminal liability under BNS, 2023, specifically under:
   a) Section 351 (Criminal Intimidation);
   b) Section 353 (Public Mischief & Incitement to commit offenses against public tranquility);
   c) Section 356 (Defamation & Damage to Reputation);
   d) Section 299 / 196 (Outraging religious sentiments / Promoting enmity between classes, if applicable).

2.1 The electronic transmission and public hosting of the impugned content violates Rule 3(1)(b) of the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, imposing a mandatory duty on platform intermediaries to disable access to objectionable digital material.

A copy of this Notice is retained in my office for future legal records and evidentiary reliance under Section 63 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA), 2023.

In a significant legal update, tech giant Google has informed the Delhi High Court that a controversial video uploaded by popular YouTuber Dhruv Rathee has been officially withheld from viewers across India. text:
Department attempts to penalise an Independent Director under GST Section 122(1A); Bombay High Court steps in to grant interim protection against coercive recovery.

Issue:
Whether an individual serving as an Independent Director of a company comes within the scope of penalty provisions under Section 122(1A) of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017, and whether interim protection against coercive recovery is warranted.

Rule:
Section 122(1A) of the CGST Act, 2017 prescribes penal liability only on any person who retains the benefit of specified fraudulent transactions or at whose instance such transactions are conducted; as judicially interpreted by the Coordinate Bench in Shantanu Sanjay Hundekari, an individual acting in a non-beneficiary or official capacity does not automatically fall under the sweep of this section.

Application:
The Assessee was subjected to penalty proceedings under Section 122(1A) in an individual capacity while serving merely as an Independent Director of the company. The Assessee contended that he was not the company itself nor did he fall within the ambit of the penal provision, relying upon the Coordinate Bench ruling which had attained finality as the Supreme Court did not interfere with it. Upon examining the statutory provision and binding precedent, the High Court observed that a strong prima facie case was established in favour of the Assessee.

Conclusion:
Since a strong prima facie case was made out by the Assessee based on established judicial precedent, the High Court granted ad-interim relief and directed the Department not to take any coercive action regarding the penalty in question until further orders.

Impact Analysis:
This order reaffirms that the Department cannot routinely invoke Section 122(1A) against independent directors or corporate professionals in their individual capacities, offering vital interim immunity from coercive tax recovery where no direct personal involvement or retention of illicit benefit is established.

Delay by Customs in re-assessing Bills of Entry and generating correct IGST challans: Bombay High Court directs Department to complete time-bound re-assessment within eight weeks with interim protection from coercive action.

Issue:
Whether the Department could be directed under writ jurisdiction to carry out re-assessment of six Bills of Entry, issue correct Integrated Goods and Services Tax (IGST) payable challans, and grant an upfront waiver of statutory interest.

Rule:
Under the provisions of the Customs Act, 1962 read with Section 3(7) of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 and the Integrated Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017, re-assessment of imported goods and determination of applicable duty/tax liability must be conducted by the proper officer in accordance with binding judicial precedents laid down by the Hon’ble Supreme Court and High Courts. Ancillary statutory levies such as interest fall within the realm of administrative adjudication during the re-assessment proceeding itself.

Application:
The Assessee approached the High Court invoking writ jurisdiction against the Department’s inaction in re-assessing six subject Bills of Entry, generating accurate IGST challans, and seeking relief against levy of interest. The Department fairly conceded to conducting the re-assessment exercise in a time-bound manner, while requesting that the claim for waiver of interest be left open for the proper officer's statutory determination. Adopting this consensus, the Court held that the re-assessment must be finalized in terms of established legal principles without the High Court delving prematurely into the merits or interest waiver.

Conclusion:
The High Court directed the Department to complete the re-assessment of the six Bills of Entry within eight weeks from the date of receipt of the certified copy of the order. While leaving the issue of interest waiver open for the proper officer to decide, the Court granted interim protection to the Assessee, directing that no coercive recovery action be initiated until the re-assessment exercise is completed.

Impact Analysis:
This ruling prevents arbitrary departmental inaction on customs re-assessments and protects importers from coercive recovery during pending adjudication, while reaffirming that statutory claims like interest waiver must first be examined by the adjudicating officer.

text: @jgopikrishnan70 NCLT order only extinguishes the personal liability of Subhash Chandra as a guarantor & doesn't wipe out the primary loans taken by the borrowing companies of Essel group (Vivek Infracon etc.). Banks & FIs can still seize & sell mortgaged assets of companies (if available).

This Subhash Chandra insolvency case does not look like a normal commercial haircut to me. The deeper you read the NCLT record, the more uncomfortable the questions become.

Let’s understand the Maths.

The easiest defence being circulated in the Subhash Chandra insolvency case is that he was “only a guarantor.” That description is legally misleading.

Under Section 128 of the Indian Contract Act, the liability of a surety is ordinarily coextensive with that of the principal debtor unless the contract provides otherwise. In simple words, a personal guarantee is not a ceremonial signature. If the borrower defaults, the creditor can proceed against the guarantor for the guaranteed liability. That is precisely why claims of around ₹22,006 crore were admitted against Subhash Chandra in his personal insolvency proceeding.

And there is another important point. He was not a man worth ₹31 crore when these guarantees were being given. The NCLT record itself refers to net worth certificates showing approximately ₹45,888 crore in 2017 and ₹40,562 crore in 2018. So the story is not that a person worth ₹31 crore somehow guaranteed ₹22,000 crore. The real story is that a promoter who had represented personal wealth of more than ₹40,000 crore gave massive guarantees, and years later, when those guarantees became enforceable, his disclosed net worth had fallen to around ₹31.79 crore.

That immediately creates the first serious question.

Where did the wealth go?

If assets worth tens of thousands of crores disappeared from the personal balance sheet, then before granting an almost complete discharge of personal liability, the natural thing should have been to trace those assets properly. Which assets were sold, to whom, for what price, where did the consideration go, whether any assets moved to relatives, group entities, LLPs, trusts or connected companies, whether those transactions were at market value and what ultimately happened to the money.

This was not merely an outside suspicion. The Technical Member herself considered the fall in net worth serious enough to call for an independent forensic audit and asset tracing exercise.

Then comes the part which, to me, makes the case even more extraordinary.

Five disputed creditors, World Crest, Lemonade, Corpcall, Veena Investments and Direct Media, together controlled around 61.78 percent of the total voting power. Their links with the Chandra and Essel ecosystem through family relationships, directorships, shareholding and corporate connections were argued before the NCLT. The Technical Member found these connections serious enough to question their voting rights. The Third Member took a narrower statutory view and said the legal test to disqualify them as associates had not been fully satisfied.

But the mathematics does not disappear.

Around 77.48 percent of the total voting share supported the plan. Remove these five disputed creditors and the support falls to around 15.70 percent, while around 18.42 percent had voted against it.

So these five were not minor creditors sitting on the side.

Their votes were decisive.

Now understand why this matters economically.

Suppose a promoter has ₹10,000 crore of personal liability. A company within the same economic ecosystem holds a ₹6,000 crore claim and an outside bank holds a ₹4,000 crore claim. The connected company accepts almost nothing on its ₹6,000 crore claim and uses its voting strength to approve the plan.

On paper it looks like that company suffered a massive loss.

But if both sides are really part of the same economic pocket, then the internal claim is only being sacrificed on paper, while the same vote helps reduce or extinguish the outside bank’s ability to recover ₹4,000 crore personally from the promoter.

That is why the real question is not who took the biggest haircut on paper.

The real question is whose money was actually lost.

If these five creditors were genuinely independent and commercially separate, then their decision is one thing. But if their economic interests were aligned with Chandra or the Essel ecosystem, then their huge nominal claims could have supplied exactly the voting power needed to cut down the personal recovery rights of outside banks.

That possibility is exactly why beneficial ownership and real economic control should have been forensically examined before approving such a massive discharge.

And there is one more fact which makes it impossible to casually say that the entire process was flawless. Claims of more than ₹185 crore on behalf of 1,260 people were admitted without proper supporting documents and later had to be excluded by the Third Member.

So no, the real issue is not simply that ₹22,006 crore became ₹6.25 crore.

The deeper issue is this.

A person once represented as worth more than ₹40,000 crore came into personal insolvency with a disclosed net worth of around ₹31.79 crore. Five disputed creditors with documented links to the wider Chandra and Essel ecosystem held 61.78 percent of the voting power. Their votes were mathematically decisive. No complete independent forensic asset tracing was done before the plan was approved.

That is why “he was only a guarantor” is not an answer.

The two questions that must be answered are very simple.

Where did the wealth go?

And who really controlled the 61.78 percent voting block?

Until these two questions are answered through a proper forensic investigation, this will not look like an ordinary commercial haircut. It will remain a serious test of whether our insolvency system can actually deal with powerful promoters, connected entities and enormous financial claims without allowing form to defeat substance.

Judgment is questionable. Thats what we are talking about.

I think this is a bad and unnecessarily narrow interpretation of the law.

Section 109(4)(b) of the IBC expressly says that a creditor who is an associate of the debtor cannot vote in the meeting of creditors. And “associate” is defined under Section 79(2). That definition contains several independent categories. It is not confined merely to whether Subhash Chandra personally owned more than 50 percent shares in these companies.

That is exactly where the interpretation becomes questionable. The Tribunal itself records that “there is no doubt” that these entities were controlled directly or indirectly by individuals related to the Personal Guarantor. Yet it then concentrates on the 50 percent ownership and formal board control test and allows them to vote.

You cannot read one clause of the definition in isolation while ignoring the other categories of associates and the admitted relationships behind these entities. The entire purpose of Section 109 is to prevent persons economically connected with the debtor from influencing the vote on the debtor’s own repayment plan.

Again, a personal guarantor is not some secondary person who becomes liable only after everything else fails. Section 128 of the Indian Contract Act makes the guarantor’s liability coextensive with that of the principal debtor, unless the contract provides otherwise. And normally, why would someone personally guarantee thousands of crores unless there is a close commercial or group interest involved?

Now look at the more troubling part. The major institutional creditors such as banks opposed the settlement, while the decisive votes came from private creditors linked directly or indirectly with Subhash Chandra. Ask a simple question. Why would an independent private lender holding claims worth thousands of crores happily accept an insignificant recovery?

That is where the suspected design becomes important. Take thousands of crores from banks, create even larger claims through associated or connected entities, gain majority voting power, and when insolvency comes, use that majority to approve a tiny settlement. The connected side effectively decides what the Personal Guarantor will pay, while institutional creditors take the loss.

Parliament specifically put Section 109 in the IBC to prevent associates from voting. The definition of associate under Section 79 is deliberately wide and the 50 percent shareholding test is only one part of it. Yet despite acknowledging links with the Personal Guarantor, the provision was interpreted so narrowly that the wider associate relationship was effectively overlooked.

This is not a small technical issue. It goes to the heart of who controlled the voting and who ultimately lost the money. And when institutional creditors lose thousands of crores, ultimately it is the money of ordinary citizens that is at stake.

Statement : The blocking of BitChat's code on GitHub is unconstitutional and authoritarian. 

New Delhi, 24 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the order issued by the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs, directing GitHub to remove the code repositories of BitChat. 

The order, Notice No. 11072601011432, was issued at 11:16 pm on 23 July 2026 under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021. The order directs GitHub to disable access to three repositories, including the Android application and its release files, within three hours. It threatens the platform with loss of safe harbour and criminal prosecution. No copy was published by the Government of India. The public learnt of it from a post by @jack, whose team develops BitChat. Censorship in India now comes to light through disclosure by the censored.

Since 17 July 2026, the Ministry of Home Affairs has suspended mobile internet around Jantar Mantar as per public reports about five times, most recently within a 1.5 kilometre radius from 4 pm until midnight on 23 July. That radius takes in Janpath and parts of Connaught Place. Reports describe signal jammers at the protest site and people walking two kilometres before their phones work. Inside that zone a student separated from her group during a detention drive cannot send a message to say where she is. Thousands of students and young people have camped at Jantar Mantar since June, seeking accountability for examination irregularities. Permission for their march to Parliament was refused. Metro stations were shut and also internet connectivity has been blocked.

BitChat is an open source application built for exactly this situation. It passes messages from phone to phone over Bluetooth, without mobile networks or a central server. It is striking that the order does not identify a single unlawful message. It objects to what BitChat is. In its own words, the application is dangerous because it enables communication "even during network restrictions" and can "circumvent lawful restrictions" during "internet shutdowns". Hence, the government's objection is that citizens can speak to one another while it has switched the internet off. 

The order is illegal on at least four grounds. 

1. Section 79(3)(b) is not a blocking power. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down the provision. Intermediaries may be required to act only on a court order, or a government notification confined to the grounds under Article 19(2) of the Constitution. Blocking is governed exclusively by Section 69A and the Blocking Rules, 2009, which require a hearing and reasons recorded in writing, subject to review. Directions issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal evade these safeguards, and constitutional challenges to this parallel regime are pending before High Courts. 

2. The reasons in the order are circular. The order asserts that the repositories contain "information which is prohibited under any law" without naming any such information, and rests on what the application is "capable of" enabling. Anticipated misuse of a communications tool is not a lawful basis to prohibit the tool. By this logic a telephone exchange could be sealed. 

3. The order cites Section 43 of the IT Act, a civil compensation provision, alongside conspiracy and abetment offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, against a platform that hosts code. 

4. A three hour deadline issued close to midnight forecloses legal assessment and recourse, and fails the proportionality standard in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637.

The order also fails on its own terms as deleting a repository does not delete the application from any phone that carries it, and the mesh keeps functioning without servers. What the takedown actually prevents is scrutiny of the underlying code.

IFF demands that the Government of India:

1. Withdraw Notice No. 11072601011432 dated 23 July 2026 issued to GitHub.

According to media reports, the Intelligence Fusion and Strategic Operations (“IFSO”) unit of the Delhi Police Special Cell has issued several notices to X, citing the IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 (“IT Rules 2021”), following complaints filed with the Delhi Police alleging circulation of “derogatory, malicious and defamatory content” targeting constitutional heads, particularly the Prime Minister, on the social media platform. The IFSO has also registered an F.I.R. under Sections 351(3), 353(2) and 356(2) of the Bharatiya Nyay Sanhita 2023, against several social media handles for posting such content.

In its “Intimation to Intermediary for Disabling Access to Unlawful Information” notices issued to X,  purportedly under provisions of IT Rules 2021, the IFSO directed the platform to:

- Delete/remove the alleged post/video from the platform immediately.

- Provide the complete registrant details including full name, address, contact details and email ID, of the X account ID holder who posted such content, as well as the login and logout details of the said account, along with corresponding time and date stamp, or any other details relevant for investigation.

 - To preserve information/ records relating to the said posts for future investigation, and furnish a certificate u/s  63(4) of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, in respect thereof.

This is not the first instance of large-scale removal of posts, as even earlier on 27 July 2026, Delhi Police reportedly instructed multiple social media intermediaries to take down posts/videos uploaded during the Jantar Mantar Protests that allegedly contained offensive or abusive remarks against the Prime Minister. Moreover, the Delhi Police’s social media monitoring team has been specifically engaged in monitoring online platforms for such content, and upon identifying objectionable posts, notices are issued to the concerned intermediaries directing them to remove the identified content.

At the outset, the legislative scheme of the IT Act 2000, does not contemplate/ permit the authorisation of the Delhi Police to direct the takedown of online content from social media platforms.

The power to block public access to online information or content is exclusively traceable to Section 69A of the IT Act 2000, which vests such power solely in the Central Government, or an officer specially authorised by it.  Whereas, Section 79(3)(b) of IT Act merely grants safe harbour to intermediaries, subject to compliance with due diligence obligations. In no circumstance can Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act 2000 or IT Rules 2021 confer a power upon the Central or State Government to devise a mechanism or appoint any agency/ officer for regulating or restricting free speech online. Reliance is placed on Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, (2015) 5 SCC 1 (para 121).

Notably, the IT (Blocking) Rules 2009 already outline procedure and rules for the designation of an officer, not below the rank of Joint Secretary, empowered to issue directions under Section 69A for blocking public access to online information. However, neither Section 69A nor the IT (Blocking) Rules, 2009 authorise the Central Government, or any State executive, to constitute a Nodal Agency empowered to direct the blocking of public access to online content.

Despite the above legislative scheme, on 26 December 2024, the Lieutenant Governor of the NCT of Delhi, purportedly in exercise of powers under the first proviso to Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT  Rules 2021 read with Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act 2000, issued a Notification appointing the Delhi Police as the Nodal Agency and Deputy Commissioners of Police (of various divisions) as designated officers for issuing takedown notices. Consequently, the Delhi Police has been issuing takedown notices pursuant to the said Notification.  However, this Notification, being founded upon a provision and subordinate legislation that do not authorise the creation of such a mechanism, is ex facie illegal and ultra vires the IT Act 2000. The legality of the said Notification has been challenged by https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 in a Petition before the Delhi High Court on the aforesaid ground, among others. The Petition is registered as W.P.(C) 7650/2025, titled “Software Freedom Law Center, India v. State of NCT of Delhi & Ors.”

Without prejudice to the aforesaid, both Section 69A and Section 79(3)(b) read with IT Rules 2021, outline overbroad grounds. While Section 69A empowers the Central Government to issue notice for blocking public access to online information on overbroad grounds such as "public order"; Section 79(3)(b) read with the IT Rules 2021 outline expansive grounds such as content’s use in the commission of an unlawful act relating to public order, decency or morality, defamation, etc., or where such information is prohibited under any prevailing law.  Since these grounds are decided by an executive order, without any judicial determination, their overbroad nature renders them susceptible to misuse and overreach. Therefore, even mere profanity, satire, or genuine criticism may be directed to be removed pursuant to such orders. This leaves the fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression vulnerable.

The risk of misuse and overreach is further exacerbated by the compliance regime applicable to intermediaries. An intermediary is likely to err on the side of over-compliance rather than independently assess the legality of a removal request, owing to the extremely limited timeline for compliance and the severe consequences of non-compliance. Under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules 2021, an intermediary is required to comply with a removal order within three hours, leaving virtually no scope for any meaningful independent assessment to guard against misuse or excessive application of such powers. Further, failure to comply exposes the intermediary to the risk of imprisonment for up to 7 years and fine for requests issued u.s. 69 A [Section 69A(3)], or the loss of safe harbour protection for orders issued u.s. 79(3)(b) [Section 79].

Moreover, when mere profanity expressed in anger against a governmental policy, or as part of political criticism, becomes the subject of penal investigation, it seriously undermines the fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression. We condemn any penal action in such circumstances, as it creates a significant chilling effect on the exercise of free speech by citizens, who are entitled to express their disagreement, dissatisfaction, or anger towards governmental policies through peaceful expression and dialogue.

Earlier today, @Meta temporarily removed Prime Minister Narendra Modi's video on the NEET paper leaks in India. According to media reports, a Meta spokesperson stated that the post was taken down due to an error and it had since been restored, post-haste.

The temporary removal of PM Modi's post highlights the larger issue of wrongful content takedowns by these platforms, often without any notice to users and leaving them with no meaningful recourse. These takedowns may be carried out by automated systems that have  been deployed as part of the growing due diligence obligations under Rule 3 of the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, or by way of government-issued order which reflects as a “legal request” on the platform.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has seen multiple instances of automated monitoring systems wrongfully taking down content, with no available recourse but engaging with the platform's internal appeals mechanisms and grievance officers. While high profile instances such as this are resolved quickly, ordinary users are often left high and dry. These issues are exacerbated by the lack of human review in the escalation process, with aggrieved users facing constant automated and AI generated responses which often fail to address even the most apparent errors in moderation. Coupled with unresponsive and inefficient grievance officer reporting procedures, users are all but helpless. Platforms may deploy these automated systems to deal with the huge volumes of content that they have to moderate under the existing regulatory system, especially since many of these obligations are tied to the safe harbour provisions under the IT Act that exempt platforms from being liable for the content they host. However, having humans in the loop for grievance redressal would ensure that fair outcomes are delivered to all and not only to high-profile persons.

According to media reports, the Delhi Police has also identified around 450 social media accounts that allegedly shared deepfakes and AI generated content related to the protests. The Delhi Police has directed social media platforms to remove this kind of content shared during the CJP protests, along with other content considered "objectionable" that relates to the Prime Minister.

Such vague orders that invoke generic grounds such as “objectionable” or “offensive” are inconsistent with the safeguards laid down in Shreya Singhal. The Supreme Court upheld Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 strictly because it required that blocking orders must be reasoned, necessary, and proportionate, and that such reasons must be recorded in writing to enable judicial review. In the present case, notices sent to social media intermediaries through the Sahyog Portal under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act and Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021, leave users in the dark, with no recourse to meaningfully challenge takedowns and leave affected parties without legal redressal. The Sahyog Portal puts in place a parallel system to take down content online, without any of the safeguards present under Section 69A.

The opacity surrounding the reasons for these takedowns goes against the strict requirements of accountability and record-keeping embedded in the Information Technology (Procedure and Safeguards for Blocking for Access of Information by Public) Rules, 2009. Instead, what we see emerging through these takedowns is a system of informal, decentralised censorship, where various government and law enforcement bodies decide the limits of free speech without transparency or oversight. An illustrative example is the temporary restriction faced by the @Cockroachisback’s primary Instagram handle, which was entirely blocked  on the evening of July 22. As per media reports, the account was restored after the Union Government reversed the blocking and advised the law enforcement agency that “action should be limited to specific posts or URLs instead of the entire account.”

It is not just the Prime Minister’s  post or CJP’s account that has faced such removals recently. Under the decentralised and opaque content removal regime, dozens of Instagram posts and videos related to the protests have been taken down, either by automated systems or in response to government orders, and many users have even had their accounts restricted. For these users, without high-profile attention, regaining access to their accounts or having the content restored is a long and arduous process, with no guarantee of remedy or reprieve.

🚨 BIG: Government of India has unveiled one of the most comprehensive legal frameworks to combat AI-generated deepfakes, synthetic media, misinformation and unlawful online content.

The framework brings together the IT Act, 2000, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, IT Rules, 2021, the 2026 IT Rules amendments, and the IndiaAI Governance Guidelines to strengthen digital safety and platform accountability.

Key highlights:

🔹 Mandatory AI Labelling: Platforms must clearly label AI-generated or synthetic content with traceable metadata so users can identify manipulated content and prevent deception.

🔹 Fastest Takedown Timelines Yet: Removal of unlawful content after a valid government or court notice has been reduced from 36 hours to just 3 hours. Grievance redressal timelines have also been tightened—from 72 hours to 36 hours, and 24 hours to 2 hours for sensitive content such as nudity, impersonation and similar categories.

🔹 IT Act, 2000: Covers penalties for computer-related offences, identity theft (Sec. 66C), online impersonation (66D), privacy violations (66E), publishing obscene or sexually explicit content (Secs. 67 & 67A), empowers blocking of unlawful content under Sec. 69A, removal directions under Sec. 79, and enables police investigation under Secs. 78 & 80.

🔹 Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: Covers cheating by personation (Sec. 319), forgery through false electronic records (Sec. 336), spreading false reports or misinformation causing public mischief (Sec. 353), and organised cybercrime involving deepfake content (Sec. 111).

🔹 Strict Platform Obligations: Intermediaries must not host or share content that infringes rights, invades privacy, promotes hate or violence, harms children, violates intellectual property, misleads users about message origin, knowingly spreads false information, impersonates individuals (including using AI), threatens India's sovereignty, security or public order, or violates any applicable law.

🔹 Greater Accountability for Social Media Platforms: Significant Social Media Intermediaries (SSMIs) must assist law enforcement in tracing originators of serious content, deploy automated tools to detect unlawful content, publish compliance reports, appoint grievance and compliance officers, maintain India-based compliance infrastructure, and provide user verification, appeals and fair hearing mechanisms.

🔹 Zero Tolerance for Harmful AI: Platforms are now explicitly required to prevent AI-generated child sexual abuse material, non-consensual intimate imagery, deepfakes, AI impersonation, harmful synthetic media and other unlawful AI-generated content using reasonable technical measures and automated detection systems.

🔹 Legal Consequences: Failure to comply with the IT Rules can result in intermediaries losing their Section 79 safe-harbour protection, exposing them to prosecution and legal action under applicable laws.

🔹 Robust Enforcement Ecosystem: The framework will be enforced through Grievance Appellate Committees (GACs), the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), the SAHYOG Portal, the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, and law enforcement agencies. Citizens can report cybercrime and deepfakes through the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, with Helpline 1930 available for cyber fraud complaints.

🔹 Responsible AI Development: Under the IndiaAI Mission, the government is funding indigenous AI safety projects, including Saakshya (IIT Jodhpur & IIT Madras), AI Vishleshak, and IIT Kharagpur's Real-Time Voice Deepfake Detection System, alongside the India AI Governance Guidelines to promote safe, trusted and responsible AI deployment.

The message is clear: AI innovation is welcome, but deepfakes, impersonation, misinformation, child exploitation, and unlawful synthetic content will face significantly stricter regulation, faster takedowns, and stronger legal consequences than ever before.

INDIA CRACKS DOWN ON AI & DEEP FAKE. BIG TECH PUT ON NOTCE

1. What has actually changed?

The Modi government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 on 10 February 2026 specifically to deal with synthetically generated information and deepfakes.
The framework covers deceptive AI-generated audio, visual and audio-visual material.
The idea is no longer simply: remove illegal content after somebody complains.

Platforms are now being pushed towards:
identification
labelling
metadata
verification
automated detection
rapid takedown
and greater accountability for allowing unlawful AI content to spread.

2. AI CONTENT HAS TO BE IDENTIFIABLE
This is probably the biggest structural change.
AI-generated/synthetically altered material covered by the rules has to be clearly identifiable as synthetic.
Platforms/services enabling generation or alteration of such content must ensure appropriate labels or traceable identifiers/metadata.
The objective is simple:
REAL CONTENT ≠ AI CONTENT
The viewer should not have to conduct a forensic investigation to figure out whether something was artificially generated.
Important nuance

Don't say “every piece of text written using AI anywhere on the internet must carry a label.”

MeitY's FAQ clarifies that the operative 2026 SGI definition primarily targets audio, visual and audio-visual information, not ordinary AI-generated written text.
A more accurate line for your video is:
“India has mandated identification and labelling requirements for covered AI-generated synthetic media, particularly deepfake audio, images and video.”

3. THE BIG NUMBER: 36 HOURS → 3 HOURS

Previously, once an intermediary received legally valid knowledge of unlawful material through the prescribed government/court process, the compliance window could be 36 hours.

That has now been cut to:

3 HOURS

That is a 91.7% reduction in response time.

So something capable of going viral nationally during an election, riot, communal incident, stock-market panic or national-security crisis can no longer theoretically remain online for a day and a half after a valid takedown direction.

The platform has only hours.

4. AND SOME COMPLAINT WINDOWS ARE EVEN SHORTER

The government says timelines for grievance redressal have also been compressed.

According to the PIB explanation:
certain complaints earlier subject to 72 hours can now require action within 36 hours

particularly sensitive categories that earlier had a 24-hour timeline can now require action within 2 hours

This specifically matters for areas such as:

impersonation

intimate imagery

nudity

deepfake abuse

other highly sensitive material.

5. BIG TECH CAN'T JUST WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT

This is another major change.

The government says intermediaries must deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures, including automated tools or other mechanisms, against unlawful synthetically generated content.
That means platforms are increasingly being pushed from:
REACTIVE MODERATION
to
PROACTIVE DETECTION
For Significant Social Media Intermediaries, the framework explicitly envisages technical measures to identify prohibited content, including certain forms of:

rape-related material

child sexual abuse material

repeat prohibited content

unlawful synthetic content.

6. USERS MAY HAVE TO DECLARE AI CONTENT

The synthetic-media framework also places responsibility upstream.

Major platforms can be required to ask users uploading covered content whether it is synthetically generated and then use technical systems to check that declaration.

So theoretically:
User uploads video →
declares AI/not AI →
platform checks →
synthetic material gets labelled.

The earlier draft framework explicitly envisaged this declaration + technical-verification model.

7. WHY THE METADATA PART MATTERS

A visible watermark can be:

cropped,
blurred,
edited,
screen-recorded,

reposted.

Metadata/identifiers create another layer of traceability.

The government's objective is therefore not merely:

“PUT AI GENERATED IN THE CAPTION.”
It is building a system where synthetic content can carry technological indicators allowing platforms to recognise what it is.
That becomes especially useful once the same manipulated video is downloaded and re-uploaded across multiple platforms.
8. THE RULES TARGET DEEPFAKE IMPERSONATION DIRECTLY
Existing IT Rules already prohibit users from publishing material that:

impersonates another person

misleads users about the origin of a message

knowingly spreads patently false or misleading information

threatens public order

violates another applicable law.

AI does not create an exemption.

If AI is being used for impersonation, fraud, defamatory fabrication or other unlawful activity, existing criminal and cyber provisions can also apply.

9. BNS CAN ALSO COME INTO PLAY
The PIB release specifically points towards provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Depending upon what the deepfake is being used for, authorities could examine provisions relating to:
Section 319 — cheating by personation
Section 336 — forgery

Section 353 — false information/rumours capable of causing public mischief or fear

Section 111 — organised crime, where the factual circumstances justify it.

So there isn't necessarily a standalone offence called simply:

“making a deepfake.”

The legal consequence depends heavily upon what the deepfake does.

10. CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE DEEPFAKES GET SPECIAL ATTENTION
This is perhaps the least discussed but most important provision.
The amended framework explicitly covers harmful AI-generated material involving:
child sexual exploitation

non-consensual intimate imagery

impersonation

other prohibited synthetic material.

Platforms are expected to prevent such content and act rapidly when detected.

11. SOCIAL-MEDIA GIANTS HAVE EXTRA DUTIES

Platforms classified as Significant Social Media Intermediaries, broadly those crossing the prescribed Indian user threshold, face additional compliance obligations.

These include mechanisms involving:
automated detection
grievance officers
compliance officers

local points of contact

India-based compliance structures

periodic compliance reports

appeals processes

originator tracing in specified circumstances for messaging services.
So the rules are aimed not only at the person creating the deepfake.
They put a major compliance burden on the distribution network itself.
12. THE REAL STICK: SAFE HARBOUR
This is where it becomes serious for Meta, X, Google, Telegram and other intermediaries.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides intermediaries conditional protection from liability for third-party content.
But that protection depends upon complying with the law and prescribed due diligence.
The PIB release reiterates that failure to observe obligations under the IT Rules can result in the intermediary losing its Section 79 exemption, after which liability can arise under applicable law.

That makes the real equation:

Comply with due diligence → retain intermediary protection

Ignore statutory obligations → safe-harbour protection can be jeopardised

That is far more powerful than merely issuing a fine.

13. GOVERNMENT HAS BUILT A TAKEDOWN PIPELINE

There is now an increasingly integrated enforcement architecture:

Grievance Appellate Committees — GACs

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre — I4C

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

14. INDIA IS ALSO BUILDING ITS OWN DEEPFAKE-DETECTION TECHNOLOGY

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras
AI Vishleshak — audio-visual forgery detection
IIT Kharagpur work on real-time voice deepfake detection.

So this is not purely a legal crackdown.

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

15. WHY THIS IS HAPPENING NOW

Generative AI has destroyed the old assumption that:
“Seeing is believing.”
Today one person can manufacture:

a politician announcing something he never said

a CEO apparently moving a stock

an Army officer issuing a fake warning

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.
And the fake can reach millions before conventional fact-checking catches up.
Therefore the Indian approach is increasingly:
IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE
rather than merely:
WAIT → RECEIVE COMPLAINT → INVESTIGATE.
THE BIG STORY FOR YOUR VIDEO

The headline isn't simply:

“Deepfakes must carry labels.”

The bigger story is that India is trying to change where responsibility lies.

Earlier, platforms could largely argue:

A user uploaded it; we are merely the intermediary.

The regulatory direction is increasingly:

If you operate the technology that generates, distributes or algorithmically amplifies synthetic content in India, you have duties to identify it, label it and respond rapidly when it becomes unlawful.

MOTION V2: A Closed Tipping System on Robinhood Chain and What It Means for Token Price

$MOTION is a social-attention / TipFi protocol token on Robinhood Chain (chain ID 4663). It is not just another meme coin. It is the unit of value inside a closed tipping network that lives on the X timeline. The newly live V2 changes how tokens enter circulation and who can receive them.

What $MOTION Is and Why V2 Matters

$MOTION runs on Robinhood Chain at token address 0xB0Fea401F1ee62F0e7cC3Bdf94b20c25aB5117e2. The main pair trades on Uniswap (pair 0x68d0ade5a861d5f09ba55565ac1a9b2c49f871fe).

The earlier beta was open. Anyone could try to farm the tip bot. The result: more than 225,000 requests in 72 hours. That system was easy to game. V2 shuts that door. The only way in now is to be tipped by an allocator — a selected account that receives a weekly allowance from the treasury. Every public tip is a soft invite into the protocol.

V2 officially went live around August 25–26, 2026. The official account @motiontip announced “V2 is Live,” along with a new app, a closed-loop system, and the principle that “every tip is an invite.”

How V2 Works (The Parts That Affect Supply)

Allocators receive 70,000 $MOTION per week. The maximum per tip is 5,000, with no daily cap inside that week. Allowance resets on Monday UTC and does not roll over. To keep the allowance, an allocator must tip on at least two separate days within seven days.

Tipping is done by replying on X with @tipmotion followed by an amount (example: @tipmotion 1000). Tipping itself costs no gas because value moves on an internal ledger. Claiming to a wallet is the only on-chain moment.

Received tips vest over 60 days (with a one-day head start, so a small slice is claimable immediately). Forwarding a tip is not bound to the same vesting schedule.

After being tipped and passing the scan at https://t.co/ZOzBBQm5NA, an account is indexed. “Bagworking” activity — relevant posts, replies, quotes, and retweets — earns points. Points accumulate per window (usually a quarter) for a pro-rata airdrop. Allocators themselves earn no points or airdrop while they hold that role.

Beta is frozen. Tip history remains visible, but beta balances cannot be claimed or carried into V2.

The treasury is a smart-account multisig on Robinhood Chain. The burn formula from the earlier era is turned off in V2 (it now evaluates to zero). New supply enters the ecosystem mainly through allocator allowances given to tip recipients.

$MOTION Price When V2 Went Live

Market data moves quickly. Based on the official pair on Dexscreener around the time of writing:

Price around $0.0077
Market cap / FDV around $7 million
Liquidity around $330 thousand
24-hour volume around $188–197 thousand
Pair age about 1 month 8 days (since roughly mid-July 2026, in line with the Robinhood Chain ecosystem)

Other aggregators have shown different prints (for example around $0.0053 with a fairly deep negative 24-hour move). That is normal for a DEX token with still-thin liquidity. Always check the live chart on Dexscreener.

Max supply is 1 billion. Most of that supply sits with the treasury for claims. Holder counts are still in the thousands, depending on the explorer or aggregator. Volatility is high: the token is early, volume is small relative to cap, and sentiment is tightly tied to tipper announcements and activity on X.

How V2 Relates to Price

V2 does not automatically “print” a higher price. What changed is the distribution mechanism and the perception of social scarcity:

More selective distribution. New tokens enter through allocator judgment, not mass farming. That reduces sell pressure from farmers who entered in beta.
An “invite-only” narrative. Every tip from a recognizable name (AvgJoesCrypto, gmoneyNFT, gabrielhaines, and others) becomes a public signal. That can attract traders who watch the social graph, not just the chart.
60-day vesting. Claims do not all hit the market at once. That dampens sudden dumps from tip recipients, at least in the short term.
Quarterly points-based airdrop. Holders and bagworkers already inside the system have a reason to stay active instead of just flipping.
The opposite risk. If allocators tip rarely, or tip accounts that sell immediately, sell pressure remains. Liquidity around $300k means a large order can still move price in a meaningful way.

In short: V2 designs the token as an incentive for a trust graph, not as an open reward. Short-term price is still set by liquidity, volume, and hype on X. Medium-term price depends more on whether allocators actually grow a network of people who produce good content rather than just farm.

Risk Notes

This is a speculative token on a new L2 with limited liquidity. Price can rise or fall sharply within hours. V2 improves the anti-farm design, but it does not remove smart-contract risk, protocol-execution risk, or general market risk. Price figures in this article are a snapshot. Always verify on Dexscreener and the explorer before making any decision.

Polymarket Signal vs Noise

What the post asserts
Secret US dredge on the Omani side created a new VLCC lane.  
Ships now pass Iran unseen.  
That is how ~750 million barrels left the Gulf.  
Therefore logistics beat missiles and the war is effectively over.

What is actually on the record
True-adjacent: CENTCOM (Adm. Cooper, ~28 Aug) said forces cleared mines from international lanes. Bessent cited large escorted oil volumes (order 100M+ bbl over weeks, not a verified 750M “because of a new canal”). 

Traffic did shift to the southern / Omani-hugging corridor during the fight; CNN and AIS shops described three routes (Iran-north, mid, Oman-south). JMIC said the Oman-side path was expanded for two-way traffic as early as June. That is routing + MCM, not a secret second strait.

False or unproven as stated: Independent writeups of the same viral package (Morse Report → JFeed / Business Today) already flag no White House / CENTCOM / Oman confirmation of a covert dredge. Charted gap Fakk al Asad / Bab Musandam is long-known, 1,600 ft / 93 ft — already in the VLCC ballpark. A hidden multi-month dredge of a “new strait” would show plant, spoil, and NOTAMs. Thread replies (including the in-thread fact-check) treat the “built a new Strait / war OVER” line as hype on top of an old channel.

Geography also kills “completely unseen”: an Omani-side lane is still inside Hormuz, still in IRGC missile/drone range. It reduces mine/central-lane risk; it does not delete Iran.

Propaganda value (channel, not truth)
This is a high-grade narrative encoder:

| Device | Function |
|---|---| ALL-CAPS secret-op + “War OVER” | Closes the story (entropy dump: \(H\to 0\) in the headline) |
| Rome / seafloor myth | Identity payoff; not a resolution source |
| Satellite-image authority | Borrows ISR prestige without a cited image chain |
| Oil barrel number | Fake precision; un-audited vs Bessent’s smaller official figures |
| 8-min video | Attention time; \(\rho\) reprint fuel |

Reach is real (~0.5M views in hours). Propaganda value is high for affect and in-group scorekeeping. It is low as a world-state update: it restates “US prefers the Oman rail + mines are clearer” in the language of a miracle canal.

IT screen from stack:

\[
I(X;Y)\approx 0 \text{ on invade / declare-war}
\]

because those contracts were never about a 1,600-ft gap. On Hormuz-normal, the real increment (mine-free claim + south routing) was already in the June–Aug tape. Benny’s increment is mostly \(J\) = framing jam:

\[
I(X;Y\mid J)\ll I(\text{CENTCOM MCM};Y)
\]

High \(\rho\) (same Morse-Report blob across accounts). \(n_{\text{eff}}\) of the cluster is small. \(I_{\text{use}}\) after \(\rho\) and “war OVER” exaggeration ≈ noise.

Market-movement assessment
| Book | Direction if someone believed the hook | Should the tape move? |
|---|---|--Hormuz normal by 30 Sep / 31 Dec | modest Yes (bypass myth) | Little. Routing + MCM already priced; “new strait” is not a resolution source |
| Invade / declare war | No (“war over”) | No. Slogan ≠ Art. I / ground ops |
| Hormuz fees / Iranian control | No | 
Weak; Oman corridor ≠ Iran giving up claims |
| Oil / risk-premium (Brent, not Poly) | down if true structural bypass | Only if AIS + official charts confirm a new cut — they haven’t |

Safe zone: do not buy Hormuz-Yes because Benny said the war is over. Do not fade mine-clearance itself — that had an official speaker. Fade the delta between “south route in use” and “America moved the seafloor.”

Read: High propaganda throughput, low mutual information. The post sells closure. The books still price a messy strait: traffic not “normal,” invasion still a low-teens–high-teens 2027 tail, no declaration of war. Treat this as a jammed reprint of CENTCOM + Oman routing, not a mover.
